node.label: Erika Rappaport
node.date_label: Shopping for Pleasure (2000) · Consuming Behaviours (coedited, 2015) · A Thirst for Empire (2017)
node.description: In Shopping for Pleasure (2000), Erika Rappaport argues that shops, clubs, restaurants and other commercial spaces helped make modern femininity and women’s urban public life in London’s West End. Consumer culture emerges through contested business practices, law, feminism and household power. A Thirst for Empire (2017) connects tea production, promotion and consumption across imperial markets. It won the American Historical Association’s 2018 Jerry Bentley Prize. Chris Nierstrasz praised its archival research and account of branding, but questioned whether its emphasis on the British Empire justified its claim to explain the modern world.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Shopping for Pleasure (2000), Rappaport uses Thompson’s account of customary protest to interpret retailers’ charivari against William Whiteley.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Licensed chapter-one opening, paragraph beginning The appearance of a charivari, note 2: “rough-shod over local custom”. Underlying Thompson text unidentified in the displayed notes and unread; specific use only.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport names Mintz’s sugar history among the resources on which her account builds.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 11: “build upon”; Mintz named. Book body and endnotes unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport names de Vries’s industrious revolution among her resources for early modern commodity history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 11: “industrious revolution”. Book body and endnotes unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport applies Beckert’s war capitalism to colonial tea cultivation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 12: “war capitalism”. Book body and endnotes unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport draws on Appleby’s contingent account of capitalism.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport identifies Appadurai’s commodity biographies as a resource for the inquiry she develops.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 13: “global biographies”. Book body and endnotes unread; bounded conceptual resource.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport follows Cooper’s advice to distinguish long-distance connections from inevitable globalization.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 15–16: “I have followed his suggestions”. Book body and endnotes unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Shopping for Pleasure (2000) explains the making of women’s urban public culture through commerce, law and contested femininity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher description, paragraphs 1–3; licensed chapter-one opening. “female urban culture”. Full book unread; a substantive contribution, not a founding claim.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the jointly authored introduction to Consuming Behaviours (2015), Rappaport, Dawson and Crowley treat consumer identities as historical and connect consumption with political regulation and international exchange.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 2–4, especially p. 3, final two paragraphs: “historical category”. Joint authorship; remainder unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Buying and Becoming (2003), Deborah Cohen reviews Erika Rappaport’s Shopping for Pleasure (2000) alongside two other books, interpreting their shared emphasis on consumption as a source of British middle-class identities, particularly women’s identities.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Only the publisher’s substantive opening extract was read. Its characterization applies collectively to three books. This records a published review, without inferring intellectual debt or a specific criticism of Rappaport from the unread remainder. Cohen is a run member.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport contributes to world history by combining comparative and connective approaches to tea’s markets and consumer cultures, foregrounding distribution and publicity in accounts of globalization.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read selected publisher-sample passages, especially pp. 14–16; the full book remains unread. This records a stated methodological intervention. Nierstrasz’s complete 2018 review was also read: he praises the research but questions whether its British-imperial concentration realizes its global ambition. No claim of comprehensive worldwide coverage is made.

proposed_edges.relationship: Christensen and Ivarsson identify A Thirst for Empire (2017) as a contribution to histories of capitalism that connects local interactions in the tea industry to global networks, while questioning its explanation of capitalism at the macro level.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the substantive discussion and surrounding argument. The authors praise the interactions she reconstructs but question capitalism’s structural specificity. Neither author has an eligible endpoint; only the field contribution is proposed.
